questions.q: What is the correct hierarchy of a CUDA kernel launch, from largest to smallest?
options: Thread, block, grid
Grid, thread, block
Grid, block, thread
Block, grid, thread
questions.explain: A kernel launch creates a grid made of blocks, and each block is made of threads — grid is the largest unit, thread the smallest.

questions.q: What does blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x compute?
options: The total number of blocks in the grid
A thread's global index across the entire grid
The number of SMs on the GPU
The size of shared memory available to the block
questions.explain: This formula flattens a thread's block position and in-block position into a single global index used to address a specific element of data.

questions.q: Why is a bounds check like `if (i < n)` needed inside many kernels?
options: Because CUDA kernels cannot use if statements
Because the number of threads launched is often rounded up and can exceed the actual data size, so extra threads must be prevented from writing out of bounds
Because blockDim.x must always equal n
Because warps require an if statement to execute at all
questions.explain: Since launches are rounded up to cover all elements (e.g. (n + 255) / 256 blocks), the last block may contain extra threads beyond the actual data size; the bounds check stops them from writing invalid memory.

questions.q: A block of threads in CUDA always runs entirely on:
options: One Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)
Multiple SMs simultaneously, split evenly
The host CPU
Whichever SM is least busy at each clock cycle, changing constantly
questions.explain: A block is assigned to and runs entirely on one SM, which is how threads within a block can cooperate through that SM's shared memory.

questions.q: Why would a kernel use a 2D grid and block configuration (dim3) instead of a flat 1D index?
options: 2D grids run faster than 1D grids on all hardware
It's required by the CUDA compiler for any kernel over 256 threads
It lets each thread map naturally to a 2D coordinate like a pixel's (x, y) position, which is more natural for image or matrix data
2D grids use less GPU memory than 1D grids
questions.explain: A 2D block/grid configuration lets each thread directly correspond to a 2D coordinate (like an image pixel), avoiding the need to manually flatten and unflatten indices.
